data: 12-hour HEO at 63.4° critical inclination — apogee parked over Russia

Molniya-1 launched 1965-04-23 from Baikonur. The 12-hour HEO at 63.4° exploits J2 apsidal lock to keep apogee dwelling over high-latitude users where geostationary satellites sit too low on the horizon. The line continued through Molniya-1/2/3, Oko early-warning, and the Meridian comms successor still in service today.
Russian 12-hour HEO comms — 63.4° critical inclination locks apogee over the north

Russian highly-eccentric orbit constellation. The 12-hour Molniya orbit (~600 × 40,000 km) at the 63.4° critical inclination exploits Earth's J2 perturbation to lock the line of apsides — apogee stays parked over the Northern Hemisphere, giving high-latitude users elevation angles a geostationary satellite can never deliver. Molniya-1 launched in 1965; the line continued through Molniya-1/2/3, the Oko early-warning satellites, and the Meridian comms successor in service today.
